title: Mexico Rejects Considering Nicaragua’s Situation a Regional Threat at the OAS
author: Arturo Sánchez Jiménez and Iván Saldaña
content:
_This article by Arturo Sánchez Jiménez and Iván Saldaña originally appeared
in the[August 19, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/08/19/politica/mexico-
rechaza-considerar-crisis-de-nicaragua-una-amenaza-regional-ante-la-oea),
Mexico’s premier left wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico Solidarity note:** Contrary to how it was framed at the OAS,
Nicaragua’s constitutional reform does not seek to annul elections. Its aim is
to eliminate foreign interference in the country’s internal political and
electoral affairs, the same principle of non-intervention that Mexico invoked
in declining to treat Nicaragua’s situation as a regional security threat.

**Mexico City.** The Mexican government warned this Wednesday that labeling
Nicaragua’s political crisis as a threat to regional security **“does not
necessarily contribute to resolving it” and may, on the contrary, “deepen the
isolation”** of the Central American country, said Mexico’s representative to
the Organization of American States (OAS), Alejandro Encinas.

In setting out Mexico’s position before the OAS Permanent Council—which voted
this morning and approved a resolution promoted by the United States to
convene a meeting of foreign ministers to discuss actions in response to the
plan by the government of Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo to abolish
elections in Nicaragua—Encinas affirmed that the Mexican government is willing
to “participate constructively” in efforts to address the political and human
rights crisis in the Central American nation.

> Para atender la situación de Nicaragua es necesario evitar medidas
> securitistas y privilegiar soluciones basadas en el diálogo, la diplomacia y
> la solución pacífica.  
> Teniendo siempre presente que las Americas son potestad exclusiva de sus
> pueblos en ejercicio pleno de su… <https://t.co/jthU0z1iWx>
>
> -- Alejandro Encinas (@A_Encinas_R) [August 19,
> 2026](https://x.com/A_Encinas_R/status/2090110835867648129?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

**However, it declined to support the US proposal** , considering that it
lacks clarity about the actions it would seek to undertake. **For that reason,
Mexico voted to abstain.**

> “Nicaragua’s internal situation does not constitute a threat to hemispheric
> peace or security.”
>
> Alejandro Encinas, Mexico’s representative to the OAS

Encinas explained that Mexico “has followed the evolution of the political and
human rights situation in Nicaragua” and reiterated the Mexican government’s
“permanent commitment” “to the promotion, protection, and respect of human
rights and fundamental freedoms.”

The diplomat recalled that the Constitution establishes the principles that
govern the country’s foreign policy: the self-determination of peoples, non-
intervention, the peaceful resolution of disputes, and unrestricted respect
for human rights.

On the basis of that framework, he said, Mexico considered that Nicaragua’s
internal situation “does not constitute a threat to hemispheric peace or
security.”

Encinas warned that characterizing the Nicaraguan crisis as a risk to regional
security “could open the door to proposing actions that exceed the powers” of
the OAS, since these are internal affairs of a state that is no longer part of
the organization.

He added that such an approach could prove incompatible with the principles of
sovereignty, self-determination, non-intervention, and the peaceful resolution
of disputes contained in the OAS Charter, the United Nations Charter, and the
American Convention on Human Rights.

Encinas stressed that Mexico does not agree with convening a consultation
meeting of foreign ministers on Nicaragua “without having clarity about what
the appropriate actions might be,” nor without a prior process of consultation
and analysis.

That path, he maintained, could steer the process away from the search for
peaceful and diplomatic solutions and orient it toward a security-focused
approach to a situation he described as “essentially political and about human
rights.”

The representative recalled the validity of the international instruments to
which Nicaragua is a party, in particular the American Convention on Human
Rights, which enshrines the right of every person to take part in “genuine,
periodic elections by universal, free, and secret suffrage.”

Encinas also cited President Claudia Sheinbaum, who, he said, has been clear
in noting that the Mexican government “always” agrees with democracy.

The diplomat reiterated Mexico’s willingness to collaborate in any process
that facilitates dialogue, promotes international cooperation for development,
and strengthens the protection of human rights in Nicaragua, “on the premise
that peace and democracy are consolidated through respect for the popular
will, sovereignty, and understanding among nations.”
